story.headline: Colombia quake toll tops 200
story.summary: The death toll from the 10 August magnitude-7.4 earthquake in western Colombia passed 200 with over 2,500 injured as rescue teams reached a final search phase.
story.display_body: The death toll from the magnitude-7.4 earthquake that struck western Colombia on Monday 10 August has climbed past 200, with more than 2,500 injured, as rescue teams moved into what officials call a final search phase. The UN said on Wednesday 12 August that it was still scaling up assistance two days after the quake, whose epicentre lay in the Chocó–Buenaventura area along the Pacific coast; humanitarian assessments continue in the hardest-hit zones around Cali, Pereira, Manizales and Quibdó, where damage to communications, transport and public services is hampering relief. UNICEF, active in Chocó for over two decades, said it had reached 22,000 people with hygiene and water-storage kits and warned that children face "growing risks" as schools and homes lie damaged and essential services stay disrupted. Two days earlier the confirmed toll stood at 111 dead and 87 injured, so the figures roughly doubled as crews reached collapsed buildings and cut-off communities.
story.why: this is Colombia's deadliest earthquake in decades, and the concentration of damage in the poorer Pacific-coast departments — where the state has a thin footprint — means recovery will test the national response long after the rescue window closes.

story.headline: Putin visits disputed Kuril Islands
story.summary: Vladimir Putin made the first-ever Russian presidential visit to the disputed Kuril Islands, drawing a formal protest from Japan.
story.display_body: Russian President Vladimir Putin made the first-ever visit by a Russian or Soviet leader to the disputed Kuril Islands, drawing a formal protest from Japan on Thursday 13 August. Putin toured a fish-processing plant on Iturup (known as Etorofu in Japan), one of four islands Tokyo claims as its "Northern Territories" and which the Soviet Union seized at the end of World War II in 1945, deporting some 17,000 Japanese residents; about 20,000 Russian citizens live there now. Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi called the visit "absolutely unacceptable" and lodged a protest through diplomatic channels. The unresolved sovereignty dispute is the reason Moscow and Tokyo never signed a formal post-war peace treaty, and relations have deteriorated further since Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
story.why: a sitting president planting himself on the contested islands is a deliberate signal that Moscow considers the question closed, hardening a territorial dispute that has blocked normal Russia–Japan relations for eight decades.

story.headline: Leavitt exits as Trump spokesperson
story.summary: Karoline Leavitt, the youngest-ever White House press secretary, will step down after about 18 months in the role.
story.display_body: Karoline Leavitt, the youngest-ever White House press secretary, will step down after about 18 months in the role, the administration announced on Wednesday 12 August. Leavitt, now 28, took the podium in January 2025 at the start of Donald Trump's second term, aged 27, and became one of the most visible defenders of the MAGA movement. In a Truth Social post Trump said she was leaving to "spend more time with her beautiful young children and family"; Leavitt, in her own statement on X, called the job "the honor and adventure of a lifetime." No successor has been named.
story.why: the press secretary is the administration's daily public voice, and losing its best-known messenger mid-term is a notable churn point — though the reasons given are personal and the podium's combative line is unlikely to change with the person behind it.

story.headline: Zambia votes on economic record
story.summary: Polls opened in Zambia's presidential election with incumbent Hakainde Hichilema seeking a second term amid widespread economic frustration.
story.display_body: Polls opened in Zambia's presidential election on Thursday 13 August, a vote turning on whether President Hakainde Hichilema's economic reforms have done enough to ease widespread hardship. Some 8.7 million registered voters have 12 hours to cast ballots; Hichilema, a 64-year-old businessman who won in 2021 on his sixth attempt, is seeking a final five-year term against a field of 13 challengers, chief among them Brian Mundubile, 55, backed by an opposition alliance rooted in the former Patriotic Front government. Inflation has eased to 6.8 percent and the kwacha has strengthened, but more than 70 percent of Zambians live on under three dollars a day, and Mundubile has alleged campaign restrictions and questioned whether the vote will be free and fair. Results are expected by 17 August, with a winner needing more than 50 percent to avoid a run-off.
story.why: Zambia is often held up as one of Africa's more stable democracies and was the first to seek debt restructuring under the G20 framework after defaulting in 2020, so how cleanly this vote runs — and whether reform survives the ballot box — carries weight well beyond its borders.

story.headline: Standerat committee weighs Mercosur deal
story.summary: A Council of States committee began hearings on the EFTA-Mercosur free-trade agreement amid a split between Swiss meat and dairy lobbies.
story.display_body: A Council of States committee began hearings on Thursday 13 August on the free-trade agreement between EFTA — the European Free Trade Association grouping Switzerland, Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein — and the South American Mercosur bloc, a deal split the Swiss farm lobby is trying to torpedo. The foreign-policy committee of the Ständerat (upper chamber) is weighing the contested agriculture file after the meat wing of the Swiss Farmers' Union helped sink the deal in a National Council vote in mid-June; the dairy sector, by contrast, backs it, seeing Mercosur's roughly 270 million consumers as an outlet for milk products Switzerland already overproduces. Mercosur — Argentina, Brazil, Uruguay, Paraguay and Bolivia — would be the most valuable of the more than 35 free-trade pacts Switzerland has signed, and business groups this week warned that letting it fail would cost export jobs.
story.why: with the US attacking the WTO-based trading order, bilaterally negotiated deals matter more to a small, export-heavy economy like Switzerland, and the farm-versus-industry fight over Mercosur is now the test case for whether Bern can still close them.

story.headline: Audit office: drug discounts skip patients
story.summary: The Federal Audit Office found only about 12 percent of an estimated 740 million francs in 2024 drug discounts reached insured patients, faulting weak federal oversight.
story.display_body: Most of the price discounts that doctors, pharmacists and hospitals get when buying medicines never reach patients, the Swiss Federal Audit Office (EFK) found in a report reported on Thursday 13 August, and it says federal oversight is too weak to fix it. Under Swiss law such rebates on prescription drugs are meant to be passed on to the insured via health insurers, with only a defined share retained for quality, training or research. The EFK estimated total discounts at about 740 million francs for 2024, of which just 88 million — around 12 percent — flowed to policyholders, leaving roughly 655 million with the providers; it judged that about half of that sum should have been passed on. The audit office faulted the Federal Office of Public Health (BAG) for lacking reliable data and effective, risk-based controls — it has agreements with only 24 percent of hospitals and 16 percent of dispensing doctors — and escalated the matter to Health Minister Elisabeth Baume-Schneider, after which the BAG agreed to add resources and tighten rules; six enforcement cases are pending.
story.why: health premiums are among the sharpest cost-of-living pressures in Switzerland, and hundreds of millions in rebates staying with providers rather than reaching insured households is exactly the kind of leakage the cost-containment drive is meant to close.

story.headline: Basel Legionella outbreak declared over
story.summary: Basel declared its Legionnaires' outbreak that killed one and sickened 28 over, confirming the source as a rooftop cooling unit at Manor's headquarters.
story.display_body: Basel's health department declared the city's Legionnaires' disease outbreak over on Thursday 13 August, saying no new cases have appeared since early August and that the source has been confirmed. The outbreak, which surfaced last week, killed one person and sickened 28; laboratory work by the cantonal laboratory and the university hospital matched bacterial strains from patients to a wet rooftop cooling unit at the Rebgasse headquarters of the Manor department-store chain, which shut the installation once the outbreak became known. One patient remains hospitalised in stable condition. Authorities cautioned that Legionella — bacteria that spread by inhaling fine contaminated water droplets, not person to person — remain a general risk, and said the canton would press at federal level for uniform national rules on managing them.
story.why: confirming the source closes the acute public-health scare and points to cooling towers as the recurring culprit, but the call for federal standards signals that Switzerland still lacks a consistent regime for a hazard that turns up repeatedly in building water systems.
